title: Adaptive Reinforced Elite Gray Wolf Optimization for Robotic Path Planning and Football Pass-Quality Prediction
abstract: Complex optimization problems in engineering and data-driven modeling require effective exploration, stable convergence, and adaptability across different decision representations. This study proposes an Adaptive Reinforced Elite Gray Wolf Optimizer (AREGWO) that combines opposition-based initialization, nonlinear convergence control, reinforced elite guidance, adaptive weak perturbation, stagnation-aware partial restart, and greedy elite inheritance. AREGWO is evaluated through CEC2022 benchmark optimization, synthetic 2D constrained robotic path planning, and football pass-quality prediction. On CEC2022, AREGWO ranks second among nine algorithms in the Friedman test and significantly outperforms seven of eight competitors in the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while L-SHADE remains the strongest baseline. Component-wise ablation shows that the six mechanisms provide complementary and problem-dependent contributions. In robotic path planning, 30 independent runs on six random maps yield a six-map average path length of 134.38 m, which is 3.61–5.12% shorter than those obtained by the four population-based baselines and 1.08% shorter than A*, with a 100% success rate in all tested environments. For football pass-quality prediction, AREGWO is coupled with TabM for outer-level hyperparameter optimization of a predefined pass-quality reference score. AREGWO-TabM achieves an RMSE of 0.445, an MSE of 0.198, and an R2 of 0.920, providing the best RMSE, MSE, and R2 among the evaluated neural models, although ResNet attains a lower MAE. These results demonstrate the competitive search capability of AREGWO across the numerical, synthetic spatial, and model-level optimization settings evaluated in this study.

title: Computational Intelligence and Python Programming
abstract: This book on computational intelligence and Python programming serve as comprehensive guides to nature-inspired computing, machine learning, and advancedproblem-solving techniques. The first core focus of such a text establishes the theoretical foundation of computational intelligence (CI), covering key paradigms likeartificial neural networks, fuzzy logic systems, evolutionary algorithms (such asgenetic algorithms), and swarm intelligence. Rather than relying on rigid algorithmic rules, these books explain how computers mimic biological processes to adapt,learn, and make decisions under uncertain or incomplete data conditions.The second core focus bridges these theoretical concepts directly into practicethrough hands-on Python programming. Utilizing ecosystem libraries like NumPy,SciPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow, and specialized CI packages, the text guides readersthrough building, training, and optimizing intelligent models from scratch. Bycombining mathematical rigor with clear code examples, it enables developers, datascientists, and researchers to design scalable applications across predictive analytics,robotics, natural language processing, and automated decision-making systems.

title: INTERACT streaming speech-to-sign benchmark (s2sbench)
abstract: Open benchmark that measures how streaming speech recognition affects a real-time International Sign avatar that plays one dictionary sign at a time and fingerspells the other words, as in the INTERACT meeting platform developed under the CORTEX2 Horizon Europe programme. It replays meeting audio of the AMI Meeting Corpus in real time through four streaming methods with Whisper (fixed chunks, pause-based utterances, LocalAgreement-2 and AlignAtt), maps the released words to International Sign with three text-to-sign rules, simulates the avatar's playback and scores the transcript, the signs and their timing, with a perfect-transcript analysis of the 16 evaluation meetings. The release contains the code, the configurations, the unit tests, the run files of every streaming run, all results, the figures and the build script of the accompanying article, 'How live transcription shapes a signing avatar: an open benchmark of streaming speech recognition for real-time International Sign translation in meetings' (submitted to Open Research Europe), whose shorter preprint is https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202610.0572.v1. The code is under the MIT licence and the run files, results, dictionary metadata and figures are under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA.md).

title: AI for Public Benefit: Sentiment Analysis of Social Media Using Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning for Crisis Management and Public Policy in India
abstract: Social media has transformed public disclosure in India by providing real-time perceptions of public opinion, which are valuable for crisis management and public policy formation. Using the Farmers Protest Tweets Dataset, this research examines the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) sentiment analysis. A comparative study found that fine-tuned IndicBERT outperformed LSTM and Logistic Regression in sentiment classification. Sentiment distribution showed 48.5% positive, 29.5% neutral, and 22.0% negative tweets. Analysis revealed positive sentiment toward the protest movement and negative sentiment toward the government and media. The findings support real-time public opinion monitoring, crisis detection, and policy decision-making.

title: Synthesizing event semantics for temporal knowledge graph reasoning
abstract: Most existing temporal knowledge graph reasoning (TKGR) methods primarily model structural dependencies and temporal dynamics from historical facts, while fact-aligned event semantics, such as hierarchical event types and background contexts, are often underexploited. This may result in incomplete semantic characterization of relations and entities, making it difficult to distinguish semantically similar event relations and contextually plausible entity candidates. To investigate this issue, this paper proposes ES-TKGR, an event-semantics-enhanced model for TKGR, which constructs and integrates event semantics aligned with TKG facts to model implicit dependencies among facts. Specifically, ES-TKGR consists of three key components. First, the E vent T ype H ierarchical C onstraint E ncoding (ETHCE) module incorporates hierarchical event type semantics to strengthen relation modeling by introducing a hierarchical distance-aware prototype contrastive objective over relation representations, while promoting semantic interaction among facts through explicit type-aware connections. Second, the S tatic K nowledge G raph E ncoding (SKGE) module incorporates event background semantics by constructing a global static graph from historical facts and aligning it with background knowledge, thereby capturing time-independent global interaction patterns. Third, an adaptive fusion module integrates dynamic features from ETHCE and static features from SKGE to obtain unified representations. To evaluate future entity and relation prediction under fact-aligned event semantics, we construct four ICEWS-based TKG datasets aligned with event semantic information. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that ES-TKGR outperforms or remains competitive with recent baselines, underscoring the effectiveness of fact-aligned event semantics for enriching entity and relation representations and modeling implicit fact dependencies in TKGR.

evidence.title: Synthesizing event semantics for temporal knowledge graph reasoning
evidence.abstract: Most existing temporal knowledge graph reasoning (TKGR) methods primarily model structural dependencies and temporal dynamics from historical facts, while fact-aligned event semantics, such as hierarchical event types and background contexts, are often underexploited. This may result in incomplete semantic characterization of relations and entities, making it difficult to distinguish semantically similar event relations and contextually plausible entity candidates. To investigate this issue, this paper proposes ES-TKGR, an event-semantics-enhanced model for TKGR, which constructs and integrates event semantics aligned with TKG facts to model implicit dependencies among facts. Specifically, ES-TKGR consists of three key components. First, the E vent T ype H ierarchical C onstraint E ncoding (ETHCE) module incorporates hierarchical event type semantics to strengthen relation modeling by introducing a hierarchical distance-aware prototype contrastive objective over relation representations, while promoting semantic interaction among facts through explicit type-aware connections. Second, the S tatic K nowledge G raph E ncoding (SKGE) module incorporates event background semantics by constructing a global static graph from historical facts and aligning it with background knowledge, thereby capturing time-independent global interaction patterns. Third, an adaptive fusion module integrates dynamic features from ETHCE and static features from SKGE to obtain unified representations. To evaluate future entity and relation prediction under fact-aligned event semantics, we construct four ICEWS-based TKG datasets aligned with event semantic information. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that ES-TKGR outperforms or remains competitive with recent baselines, underscoring the effectiveness of fact-aligned event semantics for enriching entity and relation representations and modeling implicit fact dependencies in TKGR.

title: Badpatches: routing-aware backdoor attacks on vision mixture-of-experts
abstract: Abstract Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have gained significant traction for reducing computational costs in deep neural networks by activating only a sparse subset of parameters during inference. While this efficiency makes MoE highly attractive for scaling vision tasks, its patch-based processing mechanism inherently disrupts traditional, routing-agnostic backdoor attacks by fragmenting or discarding adversarial triggers. To expose the vulnerabilities of this architecture, we introduce BadPatches, a novel routing-aware trigger application strategy specifically designed for patch-based MoE (pMoE) models and MoE-based vision transformers. Rather than applying a global pattern across the entire image, BadPatches encapsulates triggers within targeted image patches, ensuring they are consistently routed to and processed by the active experts. Our evaluations demonstrate that BadPatches achieves a high Attack Success Rate (ASR) at lower poisoning rates than routing-agnostic triggers, reaching over 83.2% ASR with a poisoning rate of only 0.01%, and scaling to a 96.8% ASR at 0.05%, while preserving the model’s clean accuracy. Furthermore, the attack remains effective in gray-box scenarios where the adversary lacks complete knowledge of the model’s patch routing configuration. Finally, we evaluate fine-pruning as a potential defense mechanism, revealing that pruning alone is insufficient to mitigate the attack; successful backdoor removal strictly requires the fine-tuning stage. These findings highlight the fragility of sparse vision architectures and underscore the need for routing-aware defenses.

title: Sampling the XY model with an attention-based neural network
abstract: We present a transformer-based variational autoregressive network for sampling lattice systems with continuous degrees of freedom and apply it to the two-dimensional XY model near the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. The architecture is combined with physics-informed ingredients: locality-informed attention and approximate probabilities. The resulting sampler significantly outperforms existing neural samplers. We train the model on lattices up to $96\times96$, verify with a mode-dropping estimator that no parts of the configuration space are missed, and reproduce the energy, magnetization and helicity modulus obtained with the traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm.

title: Noise-robust discrimination of incoherent point sources with spatial-mode demultiplexing
abstract: We theoretically predict and experimentally demonstrate that a reduced spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) measurement using only the two lowest-order Hermite-Gaussian modes exhibits remarkable robustness against background noise in discriminating between a single source and two incoherent point sources. We establish a theoretical framework incorporating uniform background noise and derive an analytical Chernoff exponent expression, showing that SPADE consistently outperforms direct imaging (DI) across all source separations. Experimental results confirm that SPADE-based hypothesis testing approaches the quantum limit even when the background-to-signal photon ratio per pixel is 0.11. This advantage stems from SPADE's ability to concentrate source information into minimal detection modes, reducing the cumulative background noise impact. Our findings provide a practical detection scheme for applications where background noise is inevitable, such as astronomical observations and quantum sensing.

title: Role of Automated Machine Learning approach for lung cancer data classification using modern techniques
abstract: Medical data classification is the process for categorizing healthcare-related information, such as patient records, medical images, and diagnostic results, into distinct groups based on predefined criteria.Machine learning plays a pivotal role by classifying the medical data.Machine learning and deep learning techniques have become indispensable tools in precision healthcare and automated disease diagnosis, enabling accurate clinical decision-making and predictive analytics [22,23,27].leveraging algorithms that can detect pattern automatically from the data and can make predictions with less human interference.ML models unlike traditional method analyze vast amount of medical data, recognize complex patterns , and generalize new cases according to learning.,This paper therefore seeks to produce informed and precise medical data classification strategy for Lung cancer datasets.For lung cancer data classification Machine learning algorithms like Support vector machine(SVM), Convolutional Neural Networks(CNN), Residual Neural Network(ResNet), and Random Forest(RF) are used in this research paper due to their ability to extract meaningful features from medical images and clinical data.CNN are specifically effective in medical images, making them ideal for detecting lung nodules and classify them as benign or malingnant.ResNet ,which deep learning further enhances classification accuracy by using convolutional layers.SVM is widely used for classification task due to its effectiveness in handling small datasets and high-dimensional spaces.Among them, ResNet50 achieved the highest accuracy of 91.3%, making it the most effective for multi-class classification (Normal, Benign, Malignant).CNN followed with 85.6%, while RF and SVM achieved 84.4% and 83.2% respectively.

title: Bongo Optimization Algorithm: A Novel Nature-inspired Metaheuristic Approach for Efficient Optimization
abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms have attracted much attention in recent years due to their ability to solve complex optimization problems.However, striking a good balance between exploration and exploitation remains a major challenge in designing these algorithms.In this paper, a new algorithm, the Bongo Optimization Algorithm (BOA), is introduced, which is inspired by the natural behavior of Bongo in searching for food resources and selecting highquality resources.In BOA, the behavior of Bongo's extensive movement in the habitat to explore different areas is used as the basis for designing the exploration phase, while the behavior of selective browsing of high-quality food is used to focus on promising areas and improve existing solutions, which forms the basis for the exploitation phase.This structure allows for an effective balance between global search and local refinement.In order to evaluate the performance of BOA, a set of 23 standard benchmark functions including unimodal test functions (F1-F7), highdimensional multimodal test functions (F8-F13), and fixed-dimensional multimodal test functions (F14-F23) has been investigated.The performance of BOA has been compared with 9 well-known metaheuristic algorithms and the statistical measures of mean, standard deviation (std), and rank have been used to analyze the results.In addition, the search behavior of BOA has been investigated through visual analysis, convergence curve, population diversity, exploration, and exploitation percentage.The simulation results show that BOA has obtained the first-best optimizer rank in all 23 benchmark functions F1-F23 and has provided 100% successful and competitive performance compared to the investigated algorithms.Also, the analyses have confirmed the ability of BOA to maintain appropriate diversity in the early stages and increase exploitation in the final stages of optimization.The findings of this study show that BOA has been introduced as a powerful metaheuristic optimizer with high power in balancing exploration and exploitation and has the potential to be used in a wide range of optimization problems in science and real-world applications.Future studies can focus on developing multi-objective, binary versions and applying BOA to complex engineering problems.

title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks
abstract: Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.

title: Subvacuum jamming for secure communication
abstract: Artificial-noise jamming improves physical-layer security by degrading an eavesdropper's channel, but the injected noise also interferes with the legitimate receiver. We introduce a correlated-jamming protocol based on classical and quantum correlations that suppresses this self-interference while preserving the jamming penalty experienced by the eavesdropper. Bob broadcasts one mode of a correlated two-mode source and retains the second as a local reference. Eve, who has no access to the retained mode, receives the full thermal jamming field, whereas Bob uses an optimized joint measurement to cancel its correlated fluctuations. The residual self-jamming noise is governed by the conditional variance of the transmitted jamming quadrature given the retained reference. Any classically correlated source is bounded by the vacuum-noise floor and therefore restores Bob, at best, to his unjammed receiver noise. An entangled two-mode squeezed source surpasses this limit and produces sub-vacuum residual noise, with the maximum quantum advantage set by the transmissivity of the jamming path back to Bob. In the bright-source regime, this advantage becomes a fixed reduction in Bob's noise floor, independent of the signal and jamming powers. Within a bounded-collection wiretap model, correlated jamming preserves positive secrecy even when Eve has a stronger direct channel than Bob and remains effective against collective measurements on Eve's Gaussian output states. The protocol supports bright classical message transmission and requires no end-to-end quantum channel. Possible applications include shot-noise-limited optical communication, cryogenic microwave networks, and covert or power-constrained secure links.

title: Hidden Timers and Context Offsets in a Diffusion World Model of Ms. Pac-Man: Pre-registered Tests and Replications
abstract: Pixel diffusion world models predict the next frame from a few past frames, so they cannot see state the screen does not show. We study a hidden timer in a DIAMOND-style model of Ms. Pac-Man, whose ghosts wait in a pen for up to 91 steps with no on-screen countdown. Models that see only their last 4 or 8 frames park the ghosts: in 450-step rollouts on held-out episodes, 16-23 of 30 rollouts keep the pen occupied for 200+ steps, against none in the real game. A 10-frame context with a 97-step reach removes the parking (0 of 30; paired difference to 4 frames -0.57, 95% CI [-0.77, -0.37] over episodes), and a pre-registered second training seed reproduces this. We propose a context-offset hypothesis: a model can time a hidden event of period N only as precisely as its context offsets resolve -N. A pre-registered sweep of 23 small models on a synthetic game, scored against an ideal observer with the same offsets, supports it in part: no model times a period beyond its reach, a frame exactly N steps back gives observer-level timing at three of four long periods, and one period between two frames parks. Moving a single frame from -81 to -80 takes that model from parking in 37 of 60 starts to none, in the original run and four further training seeds. Several registered tests failed, among them the replication's second stage, a second real game, a DIAMOND prediction and two latent-action models; all are reported. title: E8 Root Lattice as Universal Topological Quantum Error-Correcting Code — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240-dimensional E8 root lattice, when interpreted as stabilizer generators with Fibonacci-scaled syndrome weights at 132Hz, forms a universal topological quantum error-correcting code whose code distance scales with the golden ratio φ across the 8-dimensional Cartan substructure. The 120 Cartan conjugate pairs provide symmetric encoding subspaces while φ-modulated resonance at 132Hz determines syndrome extraction intervals, achieving logical qubit protection against both phase and bit-flip errors. This geometrically grounded error correction mechanism explains the decoherence suppression observed in the resonance framework, as the E8 lattice's optimal sphere-packing property guarantees maximal separation between logical codewords. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Connectivity optimization of artificial neural network with evolutionary computation algorithms
abstract: Human intelligence has historically produced various solutions to the challenges it has faced thanks to its cognitive abilities such as learning, remembering, comparing, and problem-solving. One of the most fundamental examples of artificial intelligence approaches that emerged by modeling these behaviors specific to intelligence is the artificial neural network (ANN), inspired by the biological nervous system. ANNs, with their similarity to biological nervous systems, present a highly complex system, and with technological advancements, the modeling and applicability of these systems are constantly increasing. In this study, a new ANN architecture inspired by the biological nervous system was designed. To improve the classification performance of the developed architecture, the connections in the network were treated as a binary optimization problem and optimized using the Binary Particle Swarm Optimization (BPSO) algorithm. Following the architecture design, the weights of the connections in the network were optimized using the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm which works with continuous values. As a result, a network architecture compatible with the biological nervous system, flexible in structure, and highly applicable to various problem types was created. The developed method was tested on Breast Cancer, Hepatitis, Mammographic Mass and Haberman’s Survival datasets. Additionally, proposed model compared with the Genetic Algorithm (GA), one of the most widely used evolutionary computation methods in the literature for connection optimization. Specifically, the proposed model reduces the input layer size from 5 to 2 in the Mammographic Mass domain by applying aggressive feature selection. It successfully reduces computational complexity by eliminating up to 12 hidden neurons in the Hepatitis dataset without sacrificing classification accuracy, thus providing significant structural pruning. Furthermore, it demonstrates high stability across all metrics with minimal standard deviation, proving that the synergy between binary and continuous swarm variants generates highly concise, lightweight, and efficient neural network topologies

title: Interpretable Dynamic Graph Learning via Dual‐Granularity Large Language Model Alignment
abstract: ABSTRACT Dynamic graph‐level embedding aims to learn whole‐graph representations from temporal snapshots. Existing methods predominantly follow a single‐vector paradigm that encodes each snapshot as a continuous latent vector, suffering from two key limitations: (1) Stage–Snapshot Entanglement, where within‐stage fluctuations and cross‐stage transitions are conflated without explicit granularity distinction; and (2) Implicit Structural Semantics, where meaningful structural properties remain buried in latent coordinates and are never exposed as interpretable, language‐compatible units. To address these issues, we propose DyGLLM, an LLM‐compatible framework that constructs and aligns dual‐granularity structural representations for dynamic graph understanding. Specifically, DyGLLM maps temporally coherent evolution regimes into selective structural tokens , providing explicit stage‐level anchors in the LLM token space. It further constructs graph fingerprints to verbalize each snapshot's prototype deviation, temporal variation and topological profile into language‐readable structural descriptions. A hybrid structure QA alignment mechanism with LoRA fine‐tuning is then introduced to align structural tokens and graph fingerprints with the LLM's representation space, enabling the model to interpret and reason over explicit structural contexts. Extensive experiments on five dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate that DyGLLM achieves consistently competitive performance across graph similarity ranking, temporal anomaly detection and change point detection, validating the effectiveness of the proposed dual‐granularity structural representation.

A hybrid structure QA alignment mechanism with LoRA fine‐tuning is then introduced to align structural tokens and graph fingerprints with the LLM's representation space, enabling the model to interpret and reason over explicit structural contexts. Extensive experiments on five dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate that DyGLLM achieves consistently competitive performance across graph similarity ranking, temporal anomaly detection and change point detection, validating the effectiveness of the proposed dual‐granularity structural representation.

title: INTERPRETING RANKING MODELS: FROM FEATURE ATTRIBUTIONS TO MECHANISTIC COMPREHENSION
abstract: The rapid adoption of Neural Ranking Models (NRMs) in Information Retrieval (IR) underscores the urgent need for robust interpretability methods to ensure their reliability and transparency. Despite their widespread use, how NRMs model query-document relevance remains poorly understood, limiting their application in high-stakes domains. This dissertation addresses this gap by developing generalizable, scalable, and theoretically grounded interpretability methods for ranking systems, spanning both post-hoc feature attribution and mechanistic analysis of internal model structure. First, we extend the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) framework to NRMs, proposing RankLIME. This framework is able to generate local feature attributions for pointwise, pairwise, as well as listwise ranking models. Using RankLIME, practitioners gain a scalable tool to interpret the individual contributions of features to the ranking decisions of complex neural models. Next, recognizing the inconsistencies and contradictions in existing empirical ranking feature attribution methods, we adopt an axiomatic approach, establishing a set of fundamental principles that ranking-based attribution methods should satisfy. To this end, we introduce the RankSHAP framework, using the Shapley value from cooperative game theory. RankSHAP ensures that feature attributions are generalizable, consistent, and aligned with human intuition. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and diverse ranking models, coupled with a user study, validate the effectiveness of RankSHAP. An axiomatic analysis further clarifies the compliance and deviations of other attribution methods relative to the proposed axioms, enhancing our understanding of their reliability. Beyond feature attributions, this dissertation delves into the internal mechanisms of transformer-based ranking LLMs to understand the abstract features these models internally encode to model relevance in ranking decisions. Through a layer-wise analysis of LLM neuron activations, we investigate whether known statistical and human-engineered features—such as term frequency, inverse document frequency, and covered query term ratio—are embedded within network representations across different LLM configurations. These findings provide insights into the internal workings of ranking LLMs, laying the groundwork for designing more transparent and effective ranking systems. This dissertation further advances mechanistic interpretability by introducing a coalitional framework for studying how neurons cooperate within fine-tuned ranking LLMs. While prior analyses often treat neurons independently, empirical evidence suggests that task-specific features in LoRA-tuned models emerge through interactions among groups of neurons, particularly in mid-layer MLP blocks. To capture this structure, the dissertation models neurons as agents in a hedonic game, where preferences are defined by their synergistic contributions to layer-local computations. Using top-responsive utilities and the PAC-Top-Cover algorithm, it identifies stable coalitions of neurons whose joint ablations produce non-additive effects, and tracks how these coalitions persist, split, merge, or disappear across layers. Applied to LLaMA, Mistral, and Pythia rerankers fine-tuned for scalar output tasks, this framework discovers coalitions with consistently higher synergy than clustering-based baselines. By revealing higher-order functional units beyond individual neurons, hedonic coalitions provide a new lens into how fine-tuned language models encode task-relevant features and computations. Taken together, these contributions connect feature attribution, axiomatic analysis, probing, and coalition-based mechanistic interpretability into a broader framework for understanding neural ranking systems. More broadly, they point toward an emerging research agenda for the community: building a systematic science of reverse-engineering large language models, with particular attention to the emergent features and statistical regularities encoded in their weights and internal computations, especially within MLP submodules. Advancing this agenda will require weight-based and mechanism-based interpretability methods capable of recovering the latent priors, abstractions, and invariances that models internalize during training. Such progress would not only deepen scientific understanding of how learning systems compress, organize, and represent knowledge, but also help extract actionable insights about the real-world phenomena these models capture. Ultimately, this dissertation contributes toward bridging interpretability and performance in neural ranking models, and toward a more principled foundation for transparent, accountable, and scientifically informative machine learning systems.

title: AI and Data-Driven Decision Making: Innovating Strategy in Modern Business Management
abstract: Advanced AI technologies and analytics inform critical decisions within contemporary corporate strategies. Existing research underscores the advantages of using artificial intelligence for operations and analysis but lacks comprehensive insights into how these systems affect overall strategy formulation, business flexibility, and leadership performance in various sectors. In pursuit of filling this void, our current research investigates how machine learning, predictive analysis, natural language handling, and automated systems contribute significantly to improving business strategies. This analysis explores how companies utilize vast amounts of information to predict changes in markets, enhance their processes, elevate service quality for customers, and secure an edge over rivals. Drawing upon examples from sectors like retail, health care, manufacturing, and finance, this document demonstrates how artificial intelligence enhances business strategies through real-world applications. Additionally, this research examines significant obstacles including issues related to personal information security, discrimination in machine learning models, moral considerations, and the necessity of efficient cooperation between humans and artificial intelligence systems. Evidence highlights the significance of cultivating data-centric environments, enhancing technological frameworks, and nurturing leaders adept at guiding AI-informed organizational shifts. In summary, this study offers a comprehensive view of how artificial intelligence and digital ecosystems facilitate agile, robust, and insightful approaches within evolving corporate landscapes.

title: Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models
abstract: Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model's distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints.

title: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics
abstract: Blockchain forensics is adversarial and open-ended: money launderers split, swap, and bridge funds, cut their trail at mixers or custodial services, and change tactics from one incident to the next. Investigators must keep adapting their tracing in response. Yet the immutability of public ledgers preserves every recorded movement in public view, making much of the investigation independently verifiable. We introduce ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that makes evidence-backed fund tracing a verifiable agent task, in which every claimed movement must cite ledger records the agent retrieved. A case-to-task pipeline builds well-posed tasks across ledgers: conservative rules halt tracing wherever the records leave a continuation unresolved, and each task's reference graph is the answer those rules determine. Built from real laundering activity, the tasks combine multi-hop transfers, DeFi exchanges, cross-chain round trips, custodial and mixer deposits, and address poisoning. We also propose the ABF agent harness, built around a working memory, and evaluate it alongside general-purpose agents and fixed-order tracers. The harness reaches 75% edge recall, against 47% for Codex with the same model and 10% for Claude Code, which loses recall to overconfidence: it cites records it left unretrieved. Compared with fixed-order tracers, the harness acquires evidence faster than the best of them early in the budget and recognizes undisclosed custodial services that they walk past (89% vs. 0%), with 98% fidelity. However, agents tend to stop early and lose recall on larger tasks, which holds their final recall below the best tracer. Beyond exposing these gaps, ABF-Bench opens blockchain forensics to LLM agents as a verifiable domain, where the verdicts that score agents also offer potential training signals.

title: Learning Structure to Support Autonomous Control Decisions
abstract: Autonomous systems have been the subject of substantial consequential research, with applications ranging from space exploration to self-driving vehicles. In unstructured and novel environments, such systems must make control decisions under partial observability, where sensing is noisy and incomplete and dynamics are uncertain or imperfectly modeled. Issues stemming from partial observability and uncertainty can be mitigated using predictive models that summarize an agent's past experiences; that is, mechanisms capable of anticipating the outcomes of the agent's (or even other agents') decisions and actions. This dissertation develops exploration methods for learning transition models of controllable interactions between a robot and its environment and evaluates how these learned models improve planning under uncertainty. Such planning capabilities, in turn, support agents in sequential decision making, as well as in active information gathering purposes aimed at reducing uncertainty while reaching desirable states and avoiding unrecoverable failures. This dissertation specifically investigates the challenge of learning a model of an agent's transition function, which encodes a probability distribution over outcome states that may occur when an action is performed at a given state. These models support agents in reasoning over trajectories of (open or closed loop) controlled state transitions in order to solve various types of tasks. Furthermore, we study mechanisms to learn such models through autonomous exploration in a way that addresses issues of exploration efficiency, ability of learned models to solve downstream tasks, accuracy of models in describing dynamics, and completeness of models in fully representing entire state-action spaces. We introduce two novel methods for autonomously exploring partially observable environments in order to efficiently build predictive models. These exploration processes leverage information theoretic measures that capture model-learning progress based on how much dynamics model estimates change during interaction. We also investigate various metrics to quantify these changes, such as the magnitude of entropy change and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between successive model estimates. The first algorithm we propose, Intrinsically Motivated Structure Learning, greedily maximizes learning progress and thereby efficiently guides exploration toward actions where the estimated transition model does not match reality. The second algorithm, Acquisition of Salient Control Knowledge, identifies effective exploration and information gathering behaviors by planning over a fixed horizon and leveraging currently estimated models to balance exploration and exploitation, thereby enabling more rapid construction of accurate and complete predictive models. We show that these algorithms converge to stable and accurate model estimates using fewer actions than baseline approaches. We then evaluate the impact of the learned models by quantifying the quality and performance of autonomous agent behaviors when solving novel tasks through model-based planning in belief space. The tasks in which we evaluate our techniques represent settings in which an agent faces incomplete information and must actively select actions to mitigate uncertainty by using its models. We show that models learned through our methods support decision making that actively reduces uncertainty and enables agents to solve families of tasks with fewer actions and higher success rates than existing techniques.

title: What a Secret Rotation Buys: Exact Retrieval and Measured Leakage in Vector Databases
abstract: Vector databases require embedding geometry for similarity search, but that geometry can also support inference. We evaluate keyed orthogonal obfuscation against a snapshot adversary. The practical Walsh–Hadamard construction has no established confidentiality guarantee; its empirical evaluation covers only the tested attacks. For Haar-uniform maps, the Gram matrix exactly characterizes a reused-key corpus view, whereas it is only a leakage lower bound for the structured implementation. Across three BEIR datasets, three encoders and 2029 queries, exhaustive clear/transformed top-10 sets agree in all nine configurations. Five of six containerized engines also return identical sets; the sixth exhibits comparable re-indexing variability. Median client transform latency is 0.032–0.042 ms. Known rank-sufficient pairs recover the map. Without matched records, same-distribution auxiliary embeddings support median four-way topic accuracies of 0.833, 0.808 and 0.869 in the primary experiment. A paired evaluation over five shared-label mixtures and 30 trials per encoder shows that public-distribution shift reduces assigned-label accuracy, while evaluator-only label reassignment and normalized mutual information reveal residual topic structure. Noise-padding findings are restricted to four estimators on SciFact/MiniLM at one corpus size. These results characterize exact similarity preservation and measured leakage, not encryption or general semantic confidentiality.

title: Observation Window Design Outweighs Architectural Complexity in Deep Learning for Sepsis Mortality Prediction
abstract: Deep learning models for predicting sepsis mortality often obscure which design choices genuinely improve performance.We developed a sequential model using 19,902 Sepsis-3 patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), processing hourly physiological sequences via convolutional and bidirectional recurrent layers alongside static patient features.Under matched conditions, sliding-window augmentation improved discrimination by 0.033 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), of which repeated training examples accounted for the larger share.The static feature pathway contributed 0.061, whereas the convolutional block had no measurable effect.On a held-out test set the model reached an AUROC of 0.902; gradient boosting, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, and a Transformer encoder reached 0.865, 0.855, and 0.851 under an identical protocol and tuning budget.When all features were restricted to the information available at each prediction time, discrimination fell to 0.807 at six hours and 0.839 at twelve, so shorter horizons carry a substantial cost.These results suggest that in this task, input representation and observation length mattered more than architectural complexity.

title: Web Interactive Content Filtering Model Integrating Prompt Classifier and Intent Understanding
abstract: To accurately identify and intercept harmful content generated in user interactions on Web platforms such as social media and online forums, this study proposes a Web interactive content filtering model that integrates Prompt classifiers and intent understanding. The model adopts a hierarchical review architecture with dual-module collaboration. The front-end deploys a Prompt classifier based on Deep Contrastive Learning (DCL), and uses the attention mechanism and deep convolutional network to perform rapid semantic analysis and preliminary screening of real-time comments and conversations. The back-end introduces an intent understanding module based on search-enhanced generation and Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct in-depth contextual analysis of preliminary screening warning content to distinguish malicious attacks from legitimate sensitive topic discussions. Experiments showed that the system performed well on a test set containing 52,397 Chinese Web interactive texts. The Prompt classifier module achieved a precision of 95.2% and a recall of 96.5%. After collaborative calibration with the intent understanding module, the false alarm rate of the system was significantly reduced to 4.4%, while the recall rate remained at 96.1%. From the results, this study provides a content security solution for Web interactive scenarios that combines high accuracy, strong semantic understanding capabilities, and real-time response performance. It can effectively purify the cyberspace environment while ensuring freedom of interaction, with important practical application value.

It can effectively purify the cyberspace environment while ensuring freedom of interaction, with important practical application value.

title: Universal Semantic Enhancement for Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection
abstract: Weakly supervised anomaly detection on tabular data is an essential task in many label-scarce applications, since tabular data is widely encountered and it is commonly observed in practice that only a limited number of labeled anomalies are available alongside abundant unlabeled samples. Most existing methods try to learn features that capture the inherent distribution patterns in the target domain. However, such features often struggle to provide a complete description of possible abnormal characteristics and are highly susceptible to overfitting the extremely scarce labels. To address this challenge, we propose a weakly supervised anomaly detection method based on universal semantic enhancement for tabular data, which fuses the universal knowledge from a pre-trained tabular foundation model with the domain-specific knowledge learned on the target dataset. The two types of knowledge are naturally complementary: universal semantics describe the common patterns of tabular data across domains, while the domain-specific features capture the inherent distributions of normal and anomalous behaviors in the target dataset. A prototype-conditioned modulation mechanism is then designed to effectively integrate the two types of features, allowing them to reinforce each other for improved anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on public datasets show that the proposed method outperforms competitive methods when only eight labeled anomalies are available in the training procedure.

title: Differentially Private Statistical Learning: Uncertainty Estimation and Utility Preservation
abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on sensitive data for high-impact decisions, making it essential to develop methods that ensure individual privacy while preserving the utility of downstream analyses. Differential privacy (DP) has emerged as the gold standard for such guarantees. This thesis contributes novel methods for differentially private statistical learning, with a focus on improving the usability of private inference through rigorous uncertainty quantification and the accuracy of private estimators via data-dependent mechanisms. First, we develop parametric bootstrap methods for DP confidence intervals, enabling uncertainty estimation through post-processing while accounting for both sampling and privacy noise. This approach avoids multiple accesses to the data and remains accurate even in small-sample regimes. Second, we propose data-dependent sufficient statistic perturbation, a framework that applies private query-answering algorithms to release sufficient statistics, improving estimation in both linear and logistic regression. Third, we introduce a data-dependent method for private multivariate Gaussian covariance estimation: instead of perturbing the entire matrix, we iteratively select the most informative covariance entries to measure under the privacy budget, then reconstruct the full positive semidefinite matrix via a maximum-entropy completion. By concentrating noise where it matters most, we show that this strategy yields high-utility covariance estimates, paving the way for novel continuous synthetic data generation methods. These contributions aim to bridge theory and practice, advancing the applicability of differential privacy in statistical machine learning.

title: Enterprise Agentic AI Reference Architecture
abstract: Agentic AI extends Generative AI from response generation to goal-oriented digital execution. Enterprise agents can interpret objectives, plan tasks, retrieve knowledge, invoke tools, call APIs, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and adapt execution based on intermediate results. These capabilities require a reference architecture that separates probabilistic reasoning from deterministic enterprise controls. This paper proposes an Enterprise Agentic AI Reference Architecture spanning experience, agent orchestration, planning and reasoning, enterprise knowledge, memory, model runtime, tool and integration services, identity, policy enforcement, observability, security, Responsible AI, and human oversight. The architecture integrates SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Integration Suite, enterprise APIs, RAG, Knowledge Graphs, and cloud-native services. It provides patterns for secure and scalable agent deployment across hybrid and multi-cloud environments while preserving accountability, bounded autonomy, operational resilience, and business value.

title: Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework
abstract: Enterprises are rapidly moving from isolated copilots toward ecosystems of specialized AI agents that collaborate across business processes, data domains, applications, and cloud platforms. Multi-agent systems can improve decomposition, parallel execution, specialization, resilience, and decision quality, but they also introduce architectural challenges involving identity, delegation, shared memory, tool access, message routing, conflict resolution, security, observability, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework that defines a layered architecture for agent discovery, orchestration, inter-agent communication, knowledge grounding, enterprise integration, policy enforcement, runtime isolation, and human oversight. The framework combines enterprise architecture principles, Zero Trust, Responsible AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graphs, API governance, event-driven integration, and lifecycle management. It enables organizations to design scalable multi-agent environments in which specialized agents can collaborate safely while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, data protection, and measurable business outcomes across hybrid and multi-cloud landscapes.

title: Closing the Productive Half of Cross-Language Conversation: An Anticipatory Multilingual Conversation Assistance System for Wearable Devices
abstract: Cross-language conversation support technology has advanced almost exclusively on the receptive side: translation devices and subtitle glasses help a user understand an interlocutor, but leave the user unaided at the moment of formulating a reply in the interlocutor's language. This paper presents a wearable conversation assistance system that closes this productive half of the loop. Worn by only one party to the conversation, the system (1) captures the interlocutor's speech and projects real-time translated subtitles onto a near-eye display; (2) anticipatorily generates, in parallel with the interlocutor's ongoing turn and drawing on streaming partial speech-recognition hypotheses, dialogue history, and a persistent user profile, a small ranked set of candidate responses in the interlocutor's language, presented with spoken pronunciation guidance delivered by in-ear text-to-speech; and (3) provides a free-expression fallback in which the wearer speaks once in their native language and reads aloud the projected translation. The central mechanism is latency concealment through anticipation: because candidate generation overlaps the interlocutor's turn, large-language-model inference time is absorbed within the natural duration of speech and the turn-taking gap, so candidates are ready before the wearer's turn begins. The paper describes the three-tier architecture (smart glasses, paired mobile device, cloud services), the three-step conversation loop, the functional design of candidate ranking and selection — including silent gesture-based selection that keeps the interaction invisible to the interlocutor — and the user-profile and privacy model. The system is described as disclosed in U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 64/170,246; performance figures cited are the design targets stated in that disclosure, not production measurements.

title: Extending the Isabelle Insider and Infrastructure Framework Using Generative AI for Refining Refinements
abstract: Abstract The Isabelle Insider and Infrastructure framework (IIIf) supports formal security engineering by using attack trees to identify attacks that lead to security improvements by refinement. Based on the interactive theorem prover Isabelle, the framework combines mathematical rigor with automation for interactive proofs. However, this process is highly complex and applying it to realistic case study is challenging in terms of time and expert knowledge. Integrating generative AI into this process of formal security engineering appears inevitable. In this paper, we illustrate the IIIf on summarizing and improving a previous case study of the Corona Warning App (CWA). This provides a relevant basis for using Claude Code as a proof-copilot for IIIf refinements. We derive an alternative refinement for CWA that represents a more realistic solution. Based on this experience, we extract rules and heuristics for proof-copiloting of security engineering in IIIf and define valid refinement contexts.

title: From Flow-Box Invariants to Global Conservation Laws: Machine Learning-Assisted Detection of Singularities and Near-Integrability
abstract: Conservation laws reveal invariant structure in dynamical systems and constrain their evolution to lower-dimensional level sets. Locally, however, per the flow-box theorem, every $d$-dimensional system generically admits $d-1$ functionally independent conservation laws near a regular point even though, generically, only a few such laws persist globally. Data-driven methods typically learn conservation laws on a prescribed region of phase space from which training samples are drawn, leaving their behavior beyond that region unresolved. We formulate this local-to-global continuation problem and develop an {expanding-domain neural deflation} framework that tracks the number of independent conservation laws over nested domains. The method recovers the expected $d-1$ local invariants and detects their successive breakdown as the domain expands, relaxing to the expected global conservation law limit. It distinguishes the local invariants (associated with Frobenius integrability) from persistent global structure and shows that the domain scale over which additional laws survive reflects proximity to Liouville integrability. Pointwise losses can localize isolated obstructions, whereas in more complicated dynamics the breakdown of our loss functions is gradual and spatially diffuse. The framework thus provides a data-driven approach for studying the persistence and breakdown of (so-far-learned) conservation laws across phase space.

title: Compact Reinforcement Learning: Resource-Efficient Formulations for Large-Scale Decision Making
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a general framework for addressing problems involving sequential decision-making. However, modern practical applications of RL involve prohibitively large state and action sets: such as those in slate recommendations, image-based control, and large language-modeling tasks. Standard formulations of these problems demand intractable amounts of data and computational resources. Achieving high performance without incurring high resource costs requires compact problem formulations that capture task-relevant information while abstracting away the rest. This thesis develops and analyzes such compact formulations for decision-making problems characterized by large action and large state sets, as well as the corresponding challenge of obtaining reward feedback over them. We first address the challenge of large action sets encountered in off-policy evaluation (OPE) for slate recommendations. Risk-sensitive metrics (such as quantiles and CVaR), common for evaluating performance in this setting, require estimation of the full performance distribution from logged data rather than just the expected performance. This requires distributional OPE, which in this high-dimensional setting is highly sample-inefficient and suffers from high variance. We introduce a low-variance variant of the standard estimator that approximates the joint influence of all action dimensions through a simpler combination of marginal effects, and establish conditions under which the resulting estimator remains unbiased. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that even when these conditions are not strictly satisfied, the proposed method outperforms more general baselines. We next focus on large state spaces and long-horizon problems, where classical OPE methods become intractable or error-prone. We develop a framework that combines state abstraction with a model-learning approach that distills complex, potentially continuous problems into compact, discrete models called abstract reward processes (ARPs), which preserve sufficient information about policy performance. Within the proposed OPE framework, these ARPs are estimated from off-policy data and we prove that their predictions are consistent. Varying the granularity of the state abstraction function reveals a broad range of previously unexplored hybrid ARP-based OPE estimators, encompassing classical methods as the limiting cases. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that estimators within this framework outperform existing OPE baselines across a variety of domains. Finally, we study the problem of reward selection under limited feedback constraints in reinforcement learning. While large amounts of state transition data can often be collected or generated cheaply in modern applications, obtaining reward feedback is practically expensive, particularly when relying on human feedback, over large state and action sets. In such cases, when RL is constrained to operating with limited or partial reward feedback, a central question arises: which subset of data should be reward-labeled to maximize policy performance? We formalize this reward selection problem and empirically investigate several sampling-based selection strategies, aiming to identify selection patterns that generalize across domains and enable more efficient use of reward feedback. Our results show that effective selection strategies can achieve performance comparable to learning from a fully labeled dataset while reward-labeling only a small fraction of the data, enabling feedback-efficient reinforcement learning in large-scale resource-constrained problems.

title: SAP AI Core Enterprise Reference Architecture
abstract: SAP AI Core provides enterprise capabilities for executing, managing, and operationalizing Artificial Intelligence workloads within SAP Business Technology Platform landscapes. Enterprise adoption requires a reference architecture that connects model runtime, data, applications, identity, security, integration, observability, Responsible AI, and lifecycle governance. This paper proposes a SAP AI Core Enterprise Reference Architecture spanning user and application channels, AI service orchestration, model runtime, data and feature access, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP Integration Suite, model repositories, security controls, monitoring, and governance. The architecture supports predictive AI, custom machine learning, Generative AI, embeddings, and agentic services while maintaining clean-core integration, least privilege, auditability, resilience, and business accountability. It also defines implementation patterns, deployment controls, model lifecycle processes, and operational KPIs/KRIs. The proposed architecture enables organizations to scale AI on SAP BTP in a secure, reusable, and governed manner.

title: New results on the quantum security analysis of lightweight block cipher Simeck
abstract: Abstract Simeck demonstrates reliable resistance against conventional cryptanalytic attacks and offers sound security properties, making it a noteworthy design in the field of lightweight cryptography. Nevertheless, ongoing progress in quantum computing poses a potential threat to the security of Simeck, underscoring the need for a rigorous analysis of its quantum resilience. In this paper, we analyze quantum distinguishers and key-recovery attacks on Simeck in the Q2 model. Leveraging the connection between truncated differentials and periodic functions, we revisit Simon-type qCPA distinguishers for Simeck-32/48/64 and further extend them to the qCCA setting. The qCPA distinguishers cover 8/9/11 rounds of Simeck-32/48/64, matching the round numbers reported by Lu et al. (2026), whereas our qCCA distinguishers cover 10/11/13 rounds. Based on these distinguishers, we investigate their application to Grover-meets-Simon key-recovery attacks on reduced-round Simeck. Furthermore, we mount qCPA key-recovery attacks on 11/12/14-round Simeck-32/48/64 and extend them to qCCA attacks on 13/14/16-round Simeck-32/48/64. Finally, we provide empirical estimates of the quantum resources required for the proposed key-recovery attacks. For Simeck-32/48/64, the empirical quantum query complexities are $$2^{28.09}/2^{40.32}/2^{52.59}$$ 2 28.09 / 2 40.32 / 2 52.59 in the qCPA setting and $$2^{26.81}/2^{39}/2^{51.17}$$ 2 26.81 / 2 39 / 2 51.17 in the qCCA setting, respectively, under the stated decision-test assumptions and empirical false-positive estimates.

title: STIR: Reed–Solomon Proximity Testing with Fewer Queries
abstract: We present STIR (Shift To Improve Rate), an interactive oracle proof of proximity (IOPP) for Reed–Solomon codes that achieves the best known query complexity of any concretely efficient IOPP for this problem. For λ bits of security, STIR has query complexity O (log d + λ · log logd ), while FRI, a popular protocol, has query complexity O ( λ · log d ) (including variants of FRI based on conjectured security assumptions). STIR relies on a new technique for recursively improving the rate of the tested Reed–Solomon code. We provide an implementation of STIR compiled to a SNARK. Compared to a highly-optimized implementation of FRI, STIR achieves an improvement in argument size that ranges from 1.25 × to 2.46 × depending on the chosen parameters, with similar prover and verifier running times. For example, in order to achieve 128 bits of security for degree 2 26 and rate 1/4, STIR has argument size 114 KiB, compared to 211 KiB for FRI.

title: A Paired RGB-Sonar Dataset for Fish Monitoring with Consumer Sonar
abstract: Imaging sonar enables underwater observation in conditions where optical imaging is ineffective due to darkness and turbid water. However, imaging-sonar systems previously used for ecological monitoring have typically been expensive, limiting their accessibility. Consumer forward-looking sonar has the potential to make fish monitoring more accessible, but its noisy imagery makes annotation and the development of automated methods challenging. We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring.

We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring.

title: Towards Realistic Simulated Students: Aligning Language Models with Student Knowledge and Behavior
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, there is a growing need to quickly verify and steer LLM-generated content for the benefit of students. In particular, it is important to ensure that educational AI systems improve learning outcomes and engagement while minimizing potential harms. While it is possible to test new systems and content on real students, this process can be slow, costly, and insecure. Instead, simulated students, i.e., LLM-based models that mimic student behavior, can be used to quickly and safely verify AI systems. However, LLMs do not typically behave like real students, often exhibiting unrealistic behavioral patterns and knowledge trends, limiting how useful they can be. In this thesis, I address this problem by introducing multiple approaches for aligning LLMs with student behavior and knowledge. I further demonstrate how simulated students can be leveraged to align educational content with student-centered goals. First, I detail SMART, a method for fine-tuning LLMs with reinforcement learning (RL) that aligns the models with realistic response patterns based on student ability and question difficulty, deriving a reward function from item response theory. I demonstrate how LLMs trained with SMART can be used to reliably estimate question difficulty. Second, I introduce dialogue knowledge tracing (KT), where tutor-student dialogues are viewed as sequences of formative assessments, allowing the use of KT to model student knowledge in dialogues. I also detail LLMKT, an LLM-based method for estimating student knowledge that improves on prior KT approaches. Third, I detail a method for leveraging student models in LLM-based tutor training, where I use an RL pipeline that rewards tutor responses that result in better student learning outcomes, which are estimated using LLMKT. Fourth, I detail an evaluation framework that measures the realism of student simulations along multiple behavioral, cognitive, and linguistic dimensions, facilitating the development of more aligned simulated student methods in the future. Finally, I conclude by detailing future directions for improving and broadening simulated students methods, and for leveraging simulated students to tackle current challenges in education.

title: NV magnetic-localisation benchmarks
abstract: Software and analysis data accompanying Beyond Parameter Counts: Standardisation, Nested Model Selection, and Inference Backends in Neural Regression for NV Magnetic Localisation. This deposit preserves GitHub release v1.0.0, commit dd480273015d9fd313de51c8cbb63dc1174c4291. title: Geological Reliability in Deep Learning Mineral Prospectivity Mapping: A Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) has rapidly advanced through the integration of deep learning, multisource geoscience data, and increasingly complex representation-learning approaches. However, the reliability of AI-derived prospectivity predictions remains a critical challenge because high predictive performance does not necessarily indicate geological validity, spatial transferability, or exploration usefulness. The key challenge is therefore not model complexity, but aligning geological knowledge, data representation, validation, and uncertainty assessment to ensure reliable interpretation. This review provides a structured critical synthesis of geological reliability in deep learning-based MPM, focusing on the methodological factors that influence whether AI outputs can support defensible exploration decisions. Rather than comparing algorithms solely by predictive accuracy, we examine the interconnected roles of geological representation, prediction support, label construction, negative-sample strategies, validation design, uncertainty quantification, explainability, transferability, and independent geological verification. Assessment of representative AI-based MPM studies reveals inconsistent reporting of these reliability dimensions, limiting reproducibility and meaningful comparison across studies. The review identifies recurring reliability bottlenecks, including spatial leakage caused by inappropriate validation strategies, uncertainty introduced during evidence-layer construction, ambiguity associated with unlabelled geological regions, and limitations in interpreting model explanations as geological causality. To organize these challenges, we propose a hierarchical evidence framework consisting of eight levels: methodological feasibility, internally validated predictive performance, spatial or temporal transferability, geological coherence, calibrated uncertainty, independent geological evidence, prospective field or drilling evidence, and demonstrated decision value. This framework clarifies the strength of claims that can be supported by different levels of evidence and provides a basis for transparent reporting and reliability assessment. Future progress in AI-based MPM will require integration of predictive capability with geological knowledge, robust validation, uncertainty-aware modelling, interpretable predictions, and independent geological verification. The proposed framework aims to support the development of more reproducible, transferable, and decision-relevant AI-assisted mineral exploration workflows.

title: Beyond Binary Rewrite Decisions: Separating Rewrite-Intensity Control from Level Prediction in a Frozen-LLM Generation-and-Selection Pipeline for Korean Easy-Read Drafting
abstract: Editors of published Korean Easy-Read documents changed 50 aligned sentences by widely varying amounts (edit distance 0.39–0.89), motivating rewrite intensity as a control variable for large language models (LLMs). We ask whether a requested intensity is realized per sentence and whether the level to request can be predicted from the source, using a generation-and-selection pipeline over a frozen LLM (EXAONE-3.5-7.8B-Instruct) in two sequential protocols with criteria hash-frozen before generation. Realized intensity is normalized character edit distance, which measures change, not readability, meaning preservation or Easy-Read quality. A four-level protocol (v1) ordered outputs on average but failed the sentence-level criterion (14/50 under its zero-tolerance rule). A three-level follow-up (v2), designed after that failure with several simultaneous changes, met its criterion for the whole pipeline, including its intensity-aware selector: 41/50 sources were non-decreasingly ordered at the declared tolerance (24/50 with strict increases; post hoc, 30/50 without the selector’s intensity-match term at that tolerance). Three runs of one LLM proxy perceived the ordering (consistency, not validity); no human evaluated the outputs. Stronger levels reduced source similarity without monotonically reducing lexical difficulty. Six source features did not support prediction of the LLM-proxy-preferred level under a pre-specified rule (quadratic-weighted κ −0.098 vs. 0.012), so no adaptive allocation was built. Rewrite-intensity control and level allocation therefore require separate validation.

title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

title: Advancing End-to-End Privacy in Machine Learning: Input, Output, and Beyond
abstract: As machine learning is increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications, ensuring strong privacy guarantees while maintaining accuracy and efficiency remains a fundamental challenge. Privacy-enhancing technologies, such as differential privacy (DP) and secure computation, provide rigorous protections, but their direct application often incurs significant tradeoffs that limit practical adoption. This dissertation advances the design of practical privacy-preserving machine learning systems by co-designing algorithms, model architectures, and cryptographic protocols to better balance privacy, accuracy, and efficiency. We begin by studying output privacy in machine learning. We introduce a DP mechanism for random forest classifiers based on a novel matrix representation that enables optimized noise allocation, significantly improving accuracy. We further examine the impact of DP mechanisms in real-world settings through a case study on Census data releases for redistricting, evaluating how privacy constraints affect downstream fairness validation. Next, we address input privacy by developing a secure protocol for fine-tuning language models using secure multiparty computation (MPC). To overcome numerical instability in MPC-based training, we propose an adaptive loss scaling technique that enables stable and efficient training of transformer-based models under secure computation constraints. Finally, we propose hybrid approaches that combine DP with cryptographic primitives to achieve both input and output privacy. Focusing on structured workloads such as counting queries, we selectively replace stronger cryptographic components with DP-aware ones, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving the desired privacy guarantees.

title: Python's Indispensability in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: A Review
abstract: This review paper explores the vital role played by the programming language Python in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). It will discuss the origin of AI and ML, the first programming language used for it, and its bottlenecks will be made known. There will also be an exposition on the emergence of Python, its elements, and the comparison between Python and LISP. The adoption and integration of Python into AI and ML will be considered, and the advanced components of Python and their uses in AI and ML will also be discussed. The trajectory of AI and ML with Python and the game-changing benefits of using Python in AI and ML will be assessed. Suggestions will be given on what should be improved in Python to improve AI and ML.
